text: So far, every rotation angle you've passed to a gate has been a fixed number baked straight into the circuit. Real quantum algorithms — especially the variational algorithms you'll meet in Chapter 6 — need something more flexible: a circuit template whose angles are left open, filled in later, possibly many times. That's what Parameter is for.

A plain float angle like rx of pi over 4 is fixed the moment you call it — the circuit is done. A Parameter, theta, is a symbolic placeholder instead. The circuit becomes a template: it knows it needs an RX rotation on qubit 0, but the actual angle is left unresolved until you supply one.

assign_parameters turns the template into a concrete, runnable circuit, by binding a dictionary mapping each parameter to a real number. The original template is untouched, so you can bind different values to it repeatedly — exactly the pattern a classical optimizer uses: propose an angle, bind it, run, look at the result, propose a better angle, repeat.

For an RX rotation starting from |0>, there's a clean closed-form relationship: P(1) equals sine squared of theta over 2, exact deterministic math, no sampling involved. At theta equals pi over 2, RX gives exactly the same 50/50 split as the Hadamard gate. At theta equals pi, the qubit lands on |1> with absolute certainty — the same outcome as the fixed X gate, just reached by a different, continuously tunable route.

A fixed gate like X or H is a single, specific operation — useful, but inflexible. Parameter-based rotations let an algorithm explore a continuous landscape of possible circuits by adjusting an angle, scoring the result, and adjusting again. Every variational algorithm in Chapter 6 — VQE, QAOA, and the rest — is built by wrapping exactly this bind-run-score-repeat loop around a parameterized circuit like this one.
Chapter 2 closes with a lab: building a 3-qubit GHZ state, committing to a prediction about its outcome in advance, and checking that prediction against a real simulated run.
